after: ## Background: where the ozone layer is and what it does
alt: Two atmosphere columns. With a healthy ozone layer in the lower stratosphere, most ultraviolet arrows from the Sun are absorbed and only a fraction reach the surface. With a depleted, thinner layer, more ultraviolet passes through to the surface.
caption: A thinner ozone layer absorbs less ultraviolet, so more reaches the Earth’s surface.

alt: CFCs were the propellant in aerosol spray cans and the coolant in fridges, freezers and air-conditioning. Because they are unreactive, non-flammable and non-toxic near the ground they last a long time, drift up to the stratosphere and are broken apart by ultraviolet radiation, releasing chlorine that destroys ozone.
caption: CFCs are so stable that they survive to reach the stratosphere, where they release chlorine.

alt: A chain: less ozone leads to higher levels of ultraviolet radiation at the surface. In people this damages skin cells, causing skin cancer, and the eye lens, causing cataracts. In plants it damages leaves, reducing photosynthesis and growth, so crop yields fall.
caption: Less ozone, more UV, then a named harm: skin cancer, cataracts or lower crop yields.

alt: In refrigeration CFCs were replaced first by HCFCs, which do much less damage and were a temporary step, then by HFCs and hydrocarbons, which do not deplete ozone. In aerosols pump-action sprays, roll-ons and chlorine-free propellants replaced them. HCFCs still deplete a little, HFCs are powerful greenhouse gases and hydrocarbons are flammable; the 2016 Kigali amendment phases down HFCs.
caption: Each substitute fixed the ozone problem better, but HFCs created a climate problem.

alt: Four steps: collect old fridges, freezers and air-conditioners; remove the refrigerant and CFC-containing foam; scrap the metal; destroy the CFCs at high temperature or store them securely. This stops banked CFCs leaking, but needs collection systems, specialist plants and funding, and illegal dumping still happens.
caption: Safe disposal removes CFCs from old appliances before they can leak.

alt: Three reasons the ozone strategies succeeded: practical substitutes, few producers to regulate and clear evidence of harm. Recovery is still slow because CFCs persist for decades. Compared with climate change, CFCs had cheap substitutes and few producers, whereas fossil fuels underpin whole economies.
caption: Cheap substitutes, few producers and clear evidence made ozone action work; recovery still takes decades.

alt: A line graph of October ozone at one station: 300 units in 1970, 160 in 1990, 150 in 2010 and a forecast 210 in 2030, with the 1987 Montreal Protocol marked. The fall from 1970 to 1990 is 46.7%. Values stay low after 1987 because CFCs already in the stratosphere kept destroying ozone.
caption: Ozone fell 46.7% by 1990, levelled off after the Montreal Protocol and is forecast to recover slowly.
